Oil prices rose Friday on uncertainty over Middle East supplies and a larger-than-expected draw from US ‌crude stockpiles.

US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were up about 1% to $99.07 per barrel. Brent crude, the international benchmark, was more than 1% higher $107.29.

WTI settled up more than 3% on Thursday after a big US crude stock draw on hurricane production shut-ins. For this week ​so far, Brent has increased nearly 3% while WTI has jumped 8%.

Supply jitters increased as attacks around the Strait of Hormuz surged over ​the past 10 days, with Iran saying it was stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and ‌tougher sanctions ⁠introduced last month.

European diesel refining margins declined by nearly 2% on Friday to $78.67 a barrel, after the IEA agreed on Thursday to release over 20 million barrels of diesel to the market.

Those margins rose as high as $95 a barrel in September as diesel supply tightened because of wars in Ukraine and Iran.

"Intensified Iranian attacks drove Gulf crude flows sharply lower," ​Kpler analysts said in a ​report on Thursday, adding that ⁠they expected a slower and more uneven recovery in Hormuz flows in the absence of a comprehensive political deal.

The Houthis fired missiles at Yemen's presidential palace complex in the southern ​city of Aden on Thursday, killing two guards, while the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen detailed ​dozens of ⁠attacks on Saudi infrastructure in the escalating conflict.

The Trump administration is considering lifting sanctions on some so-called shadow fleet vessels that have carried oil and petroleum products from countries such as Russia, Iran and Venezuela, in a bid to cut record global freight ⁠rates, a ​US official said on Wednesday.

The discussions come days after President Donald ​Trump temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel fuel, a move met with criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, European countries and some of Trump's fellow ​Republicans.
